section.title: Jeremiah Buys a Field
section.sectionRationale: With the Babylonian army camped outside the walls and Jeremiah himself imprisoned for prophesying the city's fall, God commands the strangest possible act of hope: buy a field. The purchase, carefully witnessed and sealed, becomes a living sign that even as Jerusalem falls, God's covenant faithfulness guarantees a future when houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in this land.
section.thesis: Jeremiah's purchase of a field he may never see again is an act of hope grounded not in the immediate circumstances, which are genuinely catastrophic, but in the character of the God for whom nothing is too difficult, whose everlasting covenant guarantees restoration on the other side of deserved judgment.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: Jeremiah imprisoned and confronted by Zedekiah for his prophecy of doom; God's command to buy the field and Jeremiah's careful, witnessed purchase; Jeremiah's own prayer wrestling with the apparent contradiction between the command and the coming disaster; God's reply naming the real reasons for Jerusalem's judgment; and God's climactic promise of an everlasting covenant and fields bought again in the land.

units.label: Jeremiah imprisoned, Zedekiah's accusation
units.note: why do you prophesy like this?

verses.text: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar.
At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard, which was in the palace of the king of Judah.

For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying: “Why are you prophesying like this? You claim that the LORD says, ‘Behold, I am about to deliver this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it.

Zedekiah king of Judah will not escape from the hands of the Chaldeans, but he will surely be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and will speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye.
He will take Zedekiah to Babylon, where he will stay until I attend to him, declares the LORD. If you fight against the Chaldeans, you will not succeed.’”
Jeremiah replied, “The word of the LORD came to me, saying:
Behold! Hanamel, the son of your uncle Shallum, is coming to you to say, ‘Buy for yourself my field in Anathoth, for you have the right of {{geullah|redemption}} to buy it.’

Then, as the LORD had said, my cousin Hanamel came to me in the courtyard of the guard and urged me, ‘Please buy my field in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for you own the right of inheritance and redemption. Buy it for yourself.’” 
Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.
So I bought the field in Anathoth from my cousin Hanamel, and I weighed out seventeen shekels of silver.
I signed and sealed the deed, called in witnesses, and weighed out the silver on the scales.
Then I took the deed of purchase, the sealed copy with its terms and conditions, as well as the open copy,

and I gave this deed to Baruch son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah, in the sight of my cousin Hanamel and the witnesses who were signing the purchase agreement and all the Jews sitting in the courtyard of the guard.
In their sight I instructed Baruch,

“This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: Take these deeds, both the sealed copy and the open copy of the deed of purchase, and put them in a clay jar to preserve them for a long time.
For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: Houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in this land.”

units.label: Jeremiah's prayer: nothing too difficult for You

verses.text: After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD:
“Oh, Lord GOD! You have made the heavens and the earth by Your great power and outstretched arm. Nothing is too {{pala|difficult}} for You!
You show loving devotion to thousands but lay the iniquity of the fathers into the laps of their children after them, O great and mighty God whose name is the LORD of Hosts,
the One great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are on all the ways of the sons of men, to reward each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.
You performed signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and You do so to this very day, both in Israel and among all mankind. And You have made a name for Yourself, as is the case to this day.
You brought Your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and with great terror.
You gave them this land that You had sworn to give their fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey.
They came in and possessed it, but they did not obey Your voice or walk in Your law. They failed to perform all that You commanded them to do, and so You have brought upon them all this disaster.

See how the siege ramps are mounted against the city to capture it. And by sword and famine and plague, the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it. What You have spoken has happened, as You now see!
Yet You, O Lord GOD, have said to me, ‘Buy for yourself the field with silver and call in witnesses, even though the city has been delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans!’”

units.label: God's reply: the real reasons for judgment

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:
“Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too difficult for Me?
Therefore this is what the LORD says: Behold, I am about to deliver this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will capture it.

And the Chaldeans who are fighting against this city will come in, set it on fire, and burn it, along with the houses of those who provoked Me to anger by burning incense to Baal on their rooftops and by pouring out drink offerings to other gods.
For the children of Israel and of Judah have done nothing but evil in My sight from their youth; indeed, they have done nothing but provoke Me to anger by the work of their hands, declares the LORD.
For this city has aroused My wrath and fury from the day it was built until now. Therefore I will remove it from My presence

because of all the evil the children of Israel and of Judah have done to provoke Me to anger, they, their kings, their officials, their priests and prophets, the men of Judah, and the residents of Jerusalem.
They have turned their backs to Me and not their faces. Though I taught them again and again, they would not listen or respond to discipline.
They have placed their abominations in the house that bears My Name, and so have defiled it.

They have built the high places of Baal in the Valley of Hinnom to make their sons and daughters pass through the fire to Molech, something I never commanded them, nor had it ever entered My mind, that they should commit such an abomination and cause Judah to sin.

units.label: An everlasting covenant, fields bought again

verses.text: Now therefore, about this city of which you say, ‘It will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword and famine and plague,’ this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says:
I will surely gather My people from all the lands to which I have banished them in My furious anger and great wrath, and I will return them to this place and make them dwell in safety.
They will be My people, and I will be their God.
I will give them one heart and one way, so that they will always fear Me for their own good and for the good of their children after them.
I will make an {{beritOlam|everlasting covenant}} with them: I will never turn away from doing good to them, and I will put My fear in their hearts, so that they will never turn away from Me.
Yes, I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will faithfully plant them in this land with all My heart and with all My soul.
For this is what the LORD says: Just as I have brought all this great disaster on this people, so I will bring on them all the good I have promised them.
And fields will be bought in this land about which you are saying, ‘It is a desolation, without man or beast; it has been delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans.’

Fields will be purchased with silver, and deeds will be signed, sealed, and witnessed in the land of Benjamin, in the areas surrounding Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, the cities of the hill country, the foothills, and the Negev, because I will restore them from captivity, declares the LORD.”

geullah.gloss: The right of redemption, the obligation of a near kinsman to buy back family land so it stays within the family, Leviticus 25:25. Jeremiah's purchase of Hanamel's field is an act of kinsman redemption at the very moment redemption itself seemed impossible.

pala.gloss: To be too difficult, too wonderful, beyond ordinary power. Jeremiah asks whether anything is too pala for the God who made heaven and earth; God answers his own question in verse 27, turning the prophet's uncertain praise into a settled promise.

beritOlam.gloss: An everlasting covenant, one God binds Himself to keep forever. Here it guarantees that God will never turn away from doing good to His people and will put His own fear in their hearts so they never turn away from Him, an unbreakable promise on the far side of a fully deserved judgment.

basic.context: With Babylon's army besieging Jerusalem and Jeremiah himself imprisoned for prophesying its fall, God commands him to buy a field from his cousin Hanamel, an act that made no earthly sense given the coming disaster. Jeremiah obeys, has the deed carefully sealed and witnessed, then honestly prays through his confusion, only to hear God explain both the real reasons for judgment and His unshakable promise of future restoration.
basic.hermeneutics: The field purchase is a prophetic sign act, a real estate transaction turned into a message: even as the city falls, God's covenant with His people has a future. Jeremiah's prayer shows that obedience and honest wrestling are not opposites; he obeys the strange command first and then brings his real confusion to God afterward.
basic.originalLanguages: Jeremiah buys the field under the ancient right of geullah, kinsman redemption, keeping family land in the family even as all land seems about to be lost. His prayer asks whether anything is too pala, too difficult, for God, and God's own answer grounds the coming beritOlam, everlasting covenant, in that same limitless power.
basic.typology: The careful, sealed, and witnessed deed preserved in a clay jar for a long time anticipates a redemption secured and guaranteed in writing, pointing forward to the certainty of the inheritance kept in Heaven for believers, 1 Peter 1:3-4. The everlasting covenant of one heart and one way anticipates the internal transformation Christ accomplishes by His Spirit.
basic.christ: Jeremiah's purchase pictures a redeemer paying a price for land under judgment because of a coming restoration he will not personally see fulfilled, a shadow of Christ, who purchased His people at the highest price while judgment was still falling, securing an inheritance He guarantees though its fullness is still to come, Ephesians 1:13-14.
basic.god: God is both perfectly just, naming with unflinching honesty the specific idolatries that have provoked His wrath, and perfectly faithful, for whom nothing is too difficult, including binding Himself to an everlasting covenant of good toward a people who have deserved only judgment.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 25:25 establishes the kinsman's right of redemption Jeremiah exercises. Ephesians 1:13-14 describes the Holy Spirit as the guarantee of an inheritance secured but not yet fully possessed. Luke 1:37, echoing Genesis 18:14, affirms that nothing is impossible with God. Ezekiel 36:26-27 parallels the promise of one heart and God's Spirit within His people.
basic.oneStory: In the darkest moment of the book, with the city already as good as fallen, God commands an act of costly, concrete hope: buy the field, because houses and fields will be bought again. That pattern, redemption purchased in the very moment judgment falls, reaches its fullest form in Christ, who purchased an everlasting inheritance for His people at the cross, guaranteed by His Spirit until its full possession.

context.literary:
Chapter 32 is built as three panels of nearly equal weight. The first is narrative, verses 1 to 15, and it moves in tight, almost legal steps: the prophet in custody, the king's accusation, a word of the LORD that predicts a visitor, the visitor arriving exactly as announced, and then the transaction itself in careful detail. The second panel is Jeremiah's prayer, verses 16 to 25, and the third is the LORD's reply, verses 26 to 44. Prayer and reply are hinged on one sentence said twice. Jeremiah says, 'Nothing is too difficult for You,' in verse 17, and God answers, 'Is anything too difficult for Me?' in verse 27. The question the prophet states as praise God hands back as a challenge, and the whole second half is the proof.

The prayer itself has a shape worth tracing. It begins with creation, verse 17, moves to God's character as both loving and just, verses 18 and 19, rehearses the exodus and the gift of the land, verses 20 to 22, and then turns on a single 'but' of disobedience in verse 23. It ends in verses 24 and 25 with the puzzle that has been sitting under every line: the siege ramps are up, the word of judgment has come true, and yet God told him to buy a field. Notice that the prayer never actually asks anything. It lays out facts and leaves a tension standing.

God's reply then answers in two movements joined by the hinge 'Now therefore' in verse 36. Verses 28 to 35 explain why the city falls, and the verb that returns three times is 'provoke Me to anger', verses 29, 30 and 32. Verses 36 to 44 explain why the field was worth buying, and they close on a balanced pair in verse 42: as God brought all this disaster, so he will bring all the good he promised. The chapter opens and closes on the same small image, property changing hands in the land, verses 15 and 43 to 44, so that the sign act frames the sermon and the sermon explains the sign.
context.historical:
The date in verse 1, the tenth year of Zedekiah and the eighteenth of Nebuchadnezzar, falls around 587 BC, and the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem had been running since the ninth year, as 2 Kings 25:1 records. The detail that Nebuchadnezzar's years and Zedekiah's years are counted side by side is itself telling. Judah is dated by the calendar of its overlord. Zedekiah had been placed on the throne by Babylon and had sworn an oath by God to serve it, 2 Chronicles 36:13, and his later revolt, leaning on Egypt, is the political background to the quarrel in verses 3 to 5.

Jeremiah is held in the courtyard of the guard, part of the royal palace complex, which was a form of detention with some freedom of access, since visitors can come and people sit there in verse 12. This is not the cistern or the dungeon of Jeremiah 37 and 38; those were worse. Anathoth, where the field lay, was Jeremiah's own village in Benjamin, Jeremiah 1:1, a priestly town to which Solomon had once exiled the priest Abiathar, 1 Kings 2:26. By this point the Babylonians would have been in control of the open country around Jerusalem, so a field there was effectively behind enemy lines. Hanamel's offer is the offer of a man trying to sell land he can no longer use, to the one relative who might be bound by duty to take it.

Silver was weighed out on scales, verse 10, because coined money was not yet in common use in Judah; the seventeen shekels were a measure of weight, about 193 grams according to the BSB note. Contracts were written on papyrus or leather, rolled, tied and sealed, with a second copy left open for ready inspection. Such double documents are known from the ancient Near East, and clay jars were a standard way to keep papers dry and safe in a hot climate. Everything about the scene is ordinary commerce, which is exactly the point the hearers would feel.
context.canonical:
The chapter sits in the middle of what readers call the Book of Consolation, Jeremiah 30 to 33, where the book that has said 'uproot and tear down' turns to the second half of its commission, 'to build and plant', Jeremiah 1:10. Verse 41 of this chapter picks up that very pair, 'I will faithfully plant them in this land', and Jeremiah 31:28 states the symmetry openly: as God watched over them to uproot, so he will watch over them to build and to plant. Chapter 32 is that promise acted out in a land deed.

Several earlier texts stand behind it. Leviticus 25:23 to 25 grounds the redemption of land in God's ownership of it, 'the land is Mine', and gives the nearest relative the duty to buy back what a poor brother has sold. The land was never meant to leave the family for good. The exodus language of verses 20 and 21, 'a strong hand and an outstretched arm', is Deuteronomy's own vocabulary, Deuteronomy 4:34 and 26:8, and the sin of verse 35 recalls the ban on giving children to Molech, Leviticus 18:21. The promise of one heart and an everlasting covenant, verses 39 and 40, runs forward into Jeremiah 31:31 to 34, Ezekiel 11:19 to 20 and 36:26 to 27, and the same phrase 'everlasting covenant' returns in Ezekiel 37:26 and Isaiah 55:3.

In the New Testament the chapter's logic of hope enacted before sight appears in Romans 8:24 and 25, 'hope that is seen is no hope at all', and its covenant promise is taken up by Paul in 2 Corinthians 6:16, which quotes the words 'I will be their God' from verse 38, as the BSB note observes. Hebrews 13:20 names the blood by which God's people are held, 'the blood of the eternal covenant'.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The narrator, Jeremiah himself speaking in the first person from verse 6, wants his hearers to see that the strange transaction was neither folly nor a private quirk. He takes care to show that the word came before the event. God told him in verse 7 that Hanamel was coming, and verse 8 records that when the cousin appeared and made the very request announced, 'Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD'. The prophet does not trust his own impulse here. He lets an outward, checkable event confirm an inward word.

The public staging serves the first hearers directly. Exiles who would later read this, and the besieged who watched it happen, needed an unforgeable sign that the destruction was not the end of the story. Witnesses signed, Baruch received the deed in the presence of all the Jews sitting in the courtyard, and the instruction was given aloud, verses 12 to 15. A private hope could be dismissed as wishful thinking, but a public, documented purchase could not. Jeremiah means his readers to be able to point to the jar.

The prayer and the reply show a second intention. Jeremiah lets the reader hear his real bewilderment, verse 25, so that no one thinks faith means feeling no tension. Then the LORD's answer teaches that both halves are true together. The hearers are not to soften the judgment, which is spelled out at length in verses 28 to 35, nor are they to give up the promise. The author wants a people who can hold both.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
What is recorded here is a one-time commission to a single man in a single siege. God told Jeremiah to buy that field from that cousin, and Jeremiah did. Nothing in the chapter tells later believers to invest in land, to draw up deeds as acts of faith, or to treat property transactions as a form of prayer. Treating it that way turns a sign into a technique.

What the narrative does hand on is a pattern of response that other parts of Scripture do command. Obey the word you have been given even when circumstances contradict it, bring your honest confusion to God in prayer rather than hiding it, and ground your confidence in who God is, creator and covenant keeper, rather than in what you can see. Paul's counsel to bring requests to God with thanksgiving fits this pattern, and Romans 8:24 and 25 describes the posture of hoping for what is not yet seen. Where the chapter describes Jeremiah's feelings, 'Yet You, O Lord GOD, have said to me', it is permission to be honest, not an instruction to cultivate doubt. Where it states God's plan, the promise of verses 37 to 44, it is binding because God spoke it, and it is addressed first to Judah's exiles, not to every reader as a personal guarantee of prosperity.

debates.question: Why does Jeremiah pray as though wrestling with God's command after he has already obeyed it?

views.label: Honest processing after obedience, not doubt before it
views.case: Jeremiah buys the field first, in verses 9 to 15, and only afterward, in verse 16, brings his honest confusion to God, modeling obedience that does not require full understanding first, followed by real wrestling in prayer.

views.label: A literary device to let God's reasoning be heard
views.case: The prayer's careful recitation of God's past power and Judah's specific sins creates the occasion for God's own extended reply in verses 26 to 44, giving the passage a structure that lets both the case for judgment and the promise of mercy be stated fully.

debates.bearing: Either way, the passage shows that obeying God's word does not require first resolving every question, and that God welcomes honest prayer even from those who have already obeyed Him.

debates.question: Does verse 18 mean children are punished for their fathers' sins?

views.label: A real principle of corporate and generational consequence
views.case: The prayer echoes Exodus 34:7, where God visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation. The judgment of 587 BC falls on a generation that inherited, and then added to, a long record of idolatry. Verse 18's own phrase, 'into the laps of their children after them', describes consequences that run down a family line.

views.label: Individual guilt is still in view
views.case: Deuteronomy 24:16 says each is to die for his own sin, and Jeremiah 31:29 and 30 explicitly retires the sour grapes proverb. Verses 19 and 23 to 35 stress that this generation, with its kings, priests and prophets, did its own evil, so the children are not suffering for sins they did not share.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not rivals. Scripture holds that sin has social and generational reach, while no one is condemned for what he did not do. Jeremiah's prayer places both on the table, and the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 promises the personal heart change that finally breaks the chain.

study.originalLanguages:
The prayer calls God's mercy chesed, verse 18, rendered 'loving devotion', and says he shows it 'to thousands'. That is a deliberate quotation of the old covenant creed in Exodus 20:6 and 34:6 to 7, where chesed to a thousand generations is set beside the visiting of iniquity on children. Jeremiah recites both halves in order, mercy then the laying of iniquity 'into the laps', a vivid Hebrew idiom that the BSB note renders 'into the bosom', the fold of the garment where one carries something close. Sin is poured into the lap of the next generation as a burden carried in the clothes. The prayer then adds that God is great in counsel and mighty in deed, verse 19, so that justice and mercy are both expressions of the same strength.

The verbs of the purchase are the language of the marketplace. Jeremiah 'weighed out' the silver, verses 9 and 10, a reminder that shekel was a unit of weight before it was a coin. He 'signed and sealed' the deed and called in witnesses. The honesty of the act is stressed by the repetition of the scales and of the open and sealed copies, where the open copy lets anyone verify what the closed copy protects against tampering.

God's promise uses a gardener's verb. 'I will faithfully plant them in this land with all My heart and with all My soul', verse 41, uses the root for planting that Jeremiah was commissioned with in Jeremiah 1:10, 'to build and plant', and that returns in 24:6, 'I will plant them and not uproot them'. The Hebrew phrase translated 'faithfully' in the BSB also carries the sense of 'in truth', so the planting is genuine and lasting. The same verse says God will rejoice in doing them good, the only place in the chapter where he is described as delighting. The judgment he must bring is spoken with heaviness, but the good is spoken with joy.

The promise 'I will give them one heart and one way', verse 39, asks to be read beside Ezekiel 11:19, where the BSB renders the parallel promise as 'singleness of heart'. In both texts the problem has been a divided heart, and God himself will supply the unity. The follow-on clause is that they will 'fear Me for their own good and for the good of their children after them', and verse 40 adds that God will put that fear in their hearts. Fear here is reverent loyalty, and the promise reverses the pattern of verse 33, where the people would not 'listen or respond to discipline'.

One more construction deserves notice. In verse 35 God says the child sacrifice 'never entered My mind', an idiom of something coming up on the heart, and the same phrase appears in Jeremiah 7:31. God disowns the practice as no part of his design, command or even imagination, which sets the whole of Judah's religion against his character.

typology.type: The nearest relative who buys back land, Jeremiah 32:7 to 9
typology.fulfillment: Under Leviticus 25:25 the nearest of kin steps in to redeem what a poor brother has lost, and Jeremiah does so at personal cost. The escalation comes in Christ, who became a brother in flesh and blood so that he could act as the one who redeems, Hebrews 2:14 to 17, and who redeems those under the law, Galatians 4:4 and 5. Where Jeremiah buys one field for one clan, Christ buys back a people and an inheritance. The type falls short because Jeremiah's purchase restores nothing at once. Christ's redemption is accomplished, though its fullness is still awaited, Romans 8:23.

typology.type: Silver weighed out on the scales, Jeremiah 32:9 to 10
typology.fulfillment: The price is counted out, exact, in front of witnesses. Peter sets the price of the greater redemption beside it, not 'perishable things such as silver or gold' but 'the precious blood of Christ', 1 Peter 1:18 and 19. The correspondence is the paying of a real cost for something that was lost. The contrast is complete: seventeen shekels could be weighed, but what Christ paid cannot be measured. The type is limited as a pointer because it shows only that redemption costs something, not who pays or what it buys.

typology.type: The everlasting covenant that will not turn away from doing good, Jeremiah 32:40
typology.fulfillment: The promise that God will 'never turn away from doing good' and will put his fear in their hearts is the core of the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31 to 34, which Jesus names at the supper, 'the new covenant in My blood', Luke 22:20. Hebrews 13:20 calls it 'the eternal covenant' sealed by blood, and Hebrews 9:15 says Christ mediates it so that the called may receive 'the promised eternal inheritance'. The earlier prophet could promise a covenant that works from within, but only Christ's death puts it in force, since a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died, Hebrews 9:16 and 17.

typology.type: Hope kept in a clay jar, Jeremiah 32:14
typology.fulfillment: The instruction that the deeds be put in a clay jar 'to preserve them for a long time' pictures a promise stored through a long wait. Paul uses the same ordinary material for something far greater, 'this treasure in jars of clay', 2 Corinthians 4:7, and Peter speaks of an inheritance that is 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven', 1 Peter 1:4. This is a modest echo and should not be pressed into allegory: the jar is not itself a symbol of Christ. It simply shows God keeping a promise safe until its time, a pattern Scripture applies to the believer's inheritance.

study.christ:
This chapter reaches Christ chiefly by way of the redeemer's role, the covenant it promises, and the pattern of costly hope. Jeremiah's field, bought from the nearest relative's obligation, belongs to the Old Testament law of redemption that Scripture uses again and again to explain what Jesus does. Hebrews 2:14 to 17 states that he 'had to be made like His brothers in every way', which is the logic of the nearest kin: only a relative may redeem. Galatians 4:4 and 5 adds that he was 'born under the law, to redeem those under the law'. Jeremiah acts for his cousin's family land. Christ acts for a family gathered from every nation, Ephesians 2:12 and 13, those once 'strangers to the covenants of the promise' who are now 'brought near through the blood of Christ'.

The covenant of verses 38 to 41 is where the chapter most clearly points ahead. 'They will be My people, and I will be their God' is the covenant formula, and the promised gift of one heart, with God putting his fear in their hearts so that they never turn away, is what Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26 and 27 describe as law written within and the Spirit placed within. Jesus holds the cup and says it is the new covenant in his blood, Luke 22:20. Hebrews 8:8 to 12 quotes Jeremiah's whole new covenant passage as fulfilled in him. What God promised he would never withdraw, 'I will never turn away from doing good to them', rests on the fact that the only covenant partner who cannot fail has taken the obligations on himself. Romans 5:19 sets the obedience of the one man against the disobedience of Adam's line, and this is the secret to why the covenant can finally be everlasting.

There is also a pattern in Jeremiah himself. A prophet, imprisoned for telling the truth, spends his money on a field he will never farm in order to say that the future belongs to God's word. Jesus likewise gave everything for an inheritance whose fullness his people still await, and Peter says the inheritance is 'reserved in heaven for you', 1 Peter 1:4. Paul calls the Spirit the 'pledge of our inheritance', Ephesians 1:14. To avoid forcing this, it should be said plainly that Jeremiah is not a disguised Christ. He is a servant whose obedient purchase bears witness to a promise whose full cost and guarantee were met only in Jesus.

Finally, God's own question in verse 27, 'Is anything too difficult for Me?', has its supreme answer in the resurrection. The angel's word to Mary in Luke 1:37 repeats Genesis 18:14, and the raising of Jesus from the dead, Hebrews 13:20, is the proof that the God who makes everlasting covenants can keep them across death itself.
study.god:
The chapter presents God as the maker whose power is the ground of everything else. 'You have made the heavens and the earth by Your great power and outstretched arm', says Jeremiah in verse 17, and God answers by calling himself 'the God of all flesh', verse 27. That title is wider than Israel. The same God who is bound to Judah by covenant is Lord of every living thing, including Nebuchadnezzar, whom the LORD names without embarrassment as the one to whom he is giving the city. Judgment by Babylon is not a defeat for God, it is his own act, verse 28.

The chapter also holds two characteristics that people often try to separate. Verse 18 gives both at once, chesed to thousands and the laying of iniquity on the next generation, and verse 19 says his eyes are on all the ways of the sons of men 'to reward each one according to his ways'. God does not drift into judgment as a mood. He sets out evidence in verses 29 to 35: incense to Baal on rooftops, drink offerings to other gods, the defiling of the temple that bears his name, and children passed through fire to Molech, 'something I never commanded'. This is a God whose anger is explained, patient in detail, and fair. He had taught them 'again and again' and they refused discipline, verse 33.

Then, after the long list of charges, comes 'Now therefore', and he turns to promise, verses 36 to 44. The turn is not forced out of him by repentance. No one in the passage repents. The promise is grounded in his own desire, 'I will rejoice in doing them good', verse 41, and in his own power to change the heart, verses 39 and 40. That is the astonishing reversal of the chapter: the God who must judge is the God who delights to do good, and he makes the good depend on himself. The pairing in verse 42, as he brought the disaster so he will bring the good, shows his word is reliable in both directions. If his threats came true, so will his promises.

For worship this means we can bring honest questions to a God who is not threatened by them. Jeremiah's prayer is long, uncertain and respectful, and God answers it fully. It also means we approach him with the sober knowledge that he takes sin seriously and with the settled confidence that his plans for his people cannot fail. His nearness is guaranteed by his own faithfulness, and nothing in the siege lines or in our circumstances is too difficult for him.

crossReferences.note: The law behind the purchase. God declares that the land is his and that his people are only residents, then gives the nearest relative the right and duty to buy back what a poor brother has sold. Jeremiah's act is the law carried out literally, at the worst possible moment, which gives the sign its weight.

Jeremiah's original commission pairs destroying with building and planting. Chapter 32 shows the second half beginning while the first is still under way, since the land deed is the opening move of the 'build and plant' promise, repeated in verse 41 and in Jeremiah 31:28.

The same rhetorical question, 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?', was put to Abraham about a child for Sarah. Jeremiah's prayer and God's reply echo it, tying the promise of a returned people to the earliest promise of a people at all.

The covenant name and character in a single declaration, compassion and loving devotion to a thousand generations beside the visiting of iniquity on children. Jeremiah's prayer in verse 18 quotes both halves, which is why mercy and judgment are held together in his plea.

The first occurrence of the claim that child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom 'did not even enter My mind'. Chapter 32:35 repeats it as the climax of Judah's sins, showing that the charge in the reply to the prayer is the same one Jeremiah had been bringing since his temple sermon.

The new covenant passage. The 'one heart', God's fear placed in their hearts and the never turning away of 32:39 to 40 are the same gifts seen from another angle, so chapter 32 is the practical, land-based sign of the covenant that chapter 31 states in principle.

God promises 'singleness of heart' and a new spirit so that they will keep his statutes, ending in 'they will be My people, and I will be their God'. This is the same formula and the same remedy as Jeremiah 32:38 to 39, spoken to the exiles in Babylon.

The 'covenant of peace' that is 'an everlasting covenant', with a sanctuary among them forever. It confirms that Jeremiah's phrase for the coming covenant belongs to a family of prophetic promises that all point to a permanent presence of God with his people.

The writer quotes Jeremiah 31's new covenant at length and applies it to the work of Christ. Because chapter 32 is the same promise acted out, Hebrews supplies the New Testament verdict that these words found their fulfillment in the better covenant.

Paul's description of hope as waiting for what is not yet seen is the inner life of Jeremiah's act. He buys the field before there is any sign of return, and Paul says that this patient hope is exactly what a believer lives by, since 'hope that is seen is no hope at all'.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a land given and held in trust. In Genesis the first humans are placed in a garden and told to tend it, and the promise to Abraham in Genesis 15 is a land, a people and a blessing for the nations. Leviticus 25 then writes that into law: the land belongs to God, and a family's portion in it cannot be lost forever. Chapter 32 arrives at the moment this whole arrangement seems to have collapsed. The people have not obeyed, the land is falling to Babylon, and the exile that Moses had warned of in Deuteronomy 28 is minutes away.

What the chapter answers from before is the question of whether the promise to Abraham survives the fall of the nation. God's reply is yes, and he says it with a deed. The people will not be dispossessed forever, because he is going to 'gather My people from all the lands to which I have banished them', verse 37, and give them again a home in safety. This is the exodus pattern running in reverse: a people carried out of the land by judgment will be carried back by grace, and the earlier rescue from Egypt, verses 20 and 21, is offered as the proof of what he can do.

What it sets up is the new covenant, the everlasting covenant of verse 40, and a heart change that the old covenant could not produce. The next stretch of the story shows the return from Babylon under Cyrus and the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and then a longer wait in which the deepest promise, one heart and one way, is still unfulfilled. The gospel announces that the wait is over in Jesus, who makes the covenant in his blood and sends the Spirit who writes God's law within, Luke 22:20 and Ezekiel 36:27.

The end of the story is the new creation, where the land promise is fulfilled beyond any one field. Revelation 21 shows a new heaven and a new earth, and a voice from the throne says 'They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God', echoing verse 38 almost word for word. Nothing is too difficult for God, not a besieged city, not a hardened people and not a dead world. Jeremiah's field, bought under the shadow of destruction, is a small, dated, signed first instalment of that future. The deed in the jar says the end of the story has already been written, and the believer's task is to live as one who has read it.

quiz.q: Why does Jeremiah buy the field in Anathoth despite the coming Babylonian conquest?

options.text: God commands it as a prophetic sign that houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in the land after the exile.
options.note: Verse 15 explicitly states the purchase is a sign of future restoration, not a wise financial decision in itself.

options.text: He believed the siege would be lifted immediately.
options.note: Jeremiah has already prophesied the city's certain fall; the purchase is a sign of future hope, not immediate deliverance.

options.text: Hanamel offered him the field for free.
options.note: Jeremiah pays seventeen shekels of silver for the field, it was not free.

options.text: It was simply a routine, unremarkable transaction with no larger significance.
options.note: The elaborate sealing, witnessing, and preservation of the deed mark this as a deliberate, significant sign act.

quiz.q: What tension does Jeremiah bring to God in his prayer in verses 16 to 25?

options.text: How buying a field could make sense when the city is already being delivered into Babylon's hands.
options.note: Verse 25 makes the tension explicit, God commanded the purchase even as the city was already falling.

options.text: Whether God actually exists.
options.note: Jeremiah's prayer affirms God's power and past deeds throughout; it does not question His existence.

options.text: Whether Hanamel had cheated him in the sale.
options.note: The prayer does not concern the fairness of the transaction but the apparent contradiction between the command and the coming disaster.

options.text: Whether he had followed the correct legal procedure for the purchase.
options.note: The legal procedure is described as carefully and correctly followed; the tension is theological, not procedural.

quiz.q: What reasons does God give for Jerusalem's coming destruction in verses 26 to 35?

options.text: Persistent idolatry, including burning incense to Baal and child sacrifice to Molech, provoking God's anger for generations.
options.note: Verses 29 to 35 specifically name these sins as the cause of the coming judgment.

options.text: God gives no reasons and the destruction is arbitrary.
options.note: God gives extensive, specific reasons rooted in Judah's persistent idolatry and disobedience.

options.text: Purely political and military failures with no moral or spiritual cause.
options.note: The stated causes are explicitly moral and spiritual, idolatry and rebellion, not merely political failure.

options.text: The actions of a single recent king alone.
options.note: The text describes sin committed by the people, their kings, officials, priests, and prophets across generations, not one king alone.

quiz.q: What does God promise in the everlasting covenant of verses 36 to 44?

options.text: He will gather His scattered people, give them one heart and one way, and never turn away from doing good to them, so fields will be bought again in the land.
options.note: Verses 37 to 44 detail this full promise of gathering, inward transformation, and restored ordinary life.

options.text: That Jerusalem will never fall to Babylon at all.
options.note: The chapter has already affirmed the city's certain fall; the everlasting covenant concerns restoration after that judgment.

options.text: That the covenant depends entirely on the people's future good behavior.
options.note: God explicitly promises He will put His fear in their hearts so they will not turn away, grounding the covenant in His own action, not merely their performance.

options.text: That only a distant future generation, with no connection to those in exile, will benefit.
options.note: The promise is to gather His people from where they have been banished, directly addressing the very generation facing exile.

quiz.q: What does the careful preservation of the sealed deed in a clay jar, verses 14 to 15, anticipate?

options.text: The certainty of a future inheritance kept secure for God's people, paralleling the Spirit as the guarantee of the believer's inheritance in Christ.
options.note: Ephesians 1:13-14 describes the Spirit as a seal and guarantee, echoing the sealed deed kept for a future, certain fulfillment.

options.text: Nothing beyond a routine legal formality of the time.
options.note: The elaborate preservation for a long time signals deliberate symbolic significance, not mere routine formality.

options.text: That the promise would never actually be fulfilled.
options.note: The whole point of preserving the deed is to testify that fields would indeed be bought again, a promise of certain fulfillment.

options.text: A warning that the field itself was worthless.
options.note: The deed's preservation testifies to the field's future value and the certainty of restoration, not worthlessness.

questions: Jeremiah bought a field he might never personally use, trusting a promise beyond his own lifetime. What costly, concrete step of hope might God be asking of you right now?
Jeremiah obeyed first and brought his honest confusion to God afterward. Where do you need to obey God before you fully understand, trusting Him with your questions along the way?
God named Judah's specific sins honestly rather than vaguely. Is there a specific sin you have been avoiding naming honestly before God?
God asked, is anything too difficult for Me, and then answered His own question with a promise of restoration. Where in your life do you need to remember that nothing is too difficult for God?
God promised to give His people one heart and one way. Where is there a divided heart in you that needs God's unifying work?

translationNotes.note: Seventeen shekels of silver was a modest price, suggesting the field's market value had already collapsed under the siege, making the purchase even more clearly an act of faith rather than sound economic investment.

Jeremiah's prayer places God's own command, buy the field, in direct tension with the visible, undeniable fact of the city's fall, a tension he brings honestly to God rather than resolving on his own before praying.

It never entered My mind underscores that child sacrifice to Molech was never God's intention or command, a practice utterly foreign to His character, directly contradicting any later claim that such rites had divine sanction.
